name: risk
title: Risk, Mitigated
kicker: What the three R's are for · ask anyone in insurance
html:
Risk, Mitigated

The riskWhat holds it down
The wrong act on the wrong stateOnly the acts the state allows, sent with its validator; a reason when absent
A different result tomorrow, given the same requestA kept script, checked against its pins on every run
A service changes, or misbehavesThe failure path the spec names, taken on purpose, and tested
A bill nobody budgetedFound once with a model, replayed with none
Nobody can say why it did thatA record of every request, answer and decision, readable by a person

Each word is a short form for more than one talk can cover: validators and lost updates, audit records, change control, cost control.

Lose any one R, and its risk comes back.
say: Ask anyone who works at an insurance company what they think about all day. Risk. Not tokens, not reasoning: risk. So let's say plainly what an agent puts at risk. It can do the wrong thing to the wrong state: merge what shouldn't be merged, pay what shouldn't be paid. It can do something different tomorrow than it did today, given the same request. It can fall over, or worse, carry on wrongly, when a service it depends on changes. It can run up a bill nobody budgeted. And when someone asks why it did what it did, there may be nothing to read. Each of those is held down by one of the R's, or by the record they leave behind. Right behavior: only the acts the current state allows, sent with the validator from the state that was read, and a reason when an act is absent. Repeatability: a kept script, checked against its pins, that does the same thing on every run and costs no tokens to repeat. Resilience: the failure paths the spec names, taken on purpose, and tested by a terrier. Lose any one of them and the risk comes back. The words are only short forms. Each stands for more than one talk can cover: validators and lost updates, audit records, change control, cost control. We'll touch a few of them today. First, though, why this matters to me, personally.

deck:ref.name: right-behavior
deck:ref.label: RIGHT-BEHAVIOR
deck:ref.title: Right behavior: only what the state allows, and a reason when not
deck:ref.summary: The agent is offered only the acts the current state allows, sends each one with the validator from the state it read, and gets a reason when an act is absent. At the small scale it is a Gherkin scenario that says what right means before any code is written.
deck:ref.cite: The first of the three R's

describedby.title: The first of the three R's

deck:ref.name: repeatability
deck:ref.label: REPEATABILITY
deck:ref.title: Repeatability: the same goal, the same result, every time
deck:ref.summary: Given the same inputs, the same outputs, call after call. Found once with a model, then replayed with none: the same steps, the same checks, the same result, until the controls really change. At the small scale it is one scenario that runs the same way every time.
deck:ref.cite: The second of the three R's

describedby.title: The second of the three R's

deck:ref.name: resilience
deck:ref.label: RESILIENCE
deck:ref.title: Resilience: the server changes, the client doesn't break
deck:ref.summary: When the server changes, or misbehaves on purpose, the client takes the failure path the spec names, re-syncs, and goes on; a model comes back only when the controls really changed, to repair. At the small scale it is the regression suite and the gates that hold, even against the model.

deck:ref.name: zta
deck:ref.label: ZTA
deck:ref.title: ZTA: Zero Token Architecture
deck:ref.summary: Agents that run inference on every call burn tokens and work against zero trust. Infer once, then run the result as reliable, deterministic code. (In my words, from the talk's page and Daniel Cranney's write-up.)
deck:ref.quote:
“You are all having way too much fun burning way too many tokens”

His opening line, as quoted in Daniel Cranney, “Infer Once, Run Everywhere: Zero-Token Architecture”, WeAreDevelopers, 13 October 2026.

deck:ref.name: ai-in-the-loop
deck:ref.label: AI-IN-THE-LOOP
deck:ref.title: AI in the loop: the person in control, the AI in support
deck:ref.summary: Natarajan, Mathur, Sidheekh, Stammer and Kersting contrast human-in-the-loop systems with AI-in-the-loop (AI²L) systems, where the human is in control of the system and the AI is there to support the human, and argue that evaluations should not judge the machine component alone.
deck:ref.quote: “We argue that existing evaluation methods often overemphasize the machine (learning) component's performance, neglecting the human expert's critical role.”
deck:ref.cite: Natarajan, Mathur, Sidheekh, Stammer and Kersting, “Human-in-the-loop or AI-in-the-loop? Automate or Collaborate?”, arXiv

describedby.title: Natarajan, Mathur, Sidheekh, Stammer and Kersting, “Human-in-the-loop or AI-in-the-loop? Automate or Collaborate?”, arXiv

deck:ref.name: reliability
deck:ref.label: RELIABILITY
deck:ref.title: Reliability: what the three R's add up to
deck:ref.summary: Not a fourth R beside the others: the one over them. A system is reliable only when it behaves right, repeats that behavior given the same inputs, and stays right when things change or break. Miss any one and it isn't.

deck:ref.name: risk
deck:ref.label: RISK
deck:ref.title: Risk, mitigated: what reliability buys
deck:ref.summary: Wrong acts on the wrong state, drift between runs, surprises when a service changes, unbounded spend, decisions nobody can reconstruct. Each is a risk; each is held down by one of the R's, or by the record they leave. Lose an R and the risk comes back.
